report.source_text: Anticoagulation treatment with infusion of high molecular weight heparin was introduced. The dosage was modified according to APPT with a target level of 70–85 s. Glucocorticoids: methyprednisolon 1 g i.v. for three consecutive days, followed by prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (60 mg/day) were also used. Therapeutic plasma exchanges were added to remove antiphospholipid antibodies. Because of severe renal insufficiency with anuria, fluid overload with respiratory failure, daily hemodialysis treatment was introduced. Systemic antibiotic therapy with piperacyllin/tazobactam was also added.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 35-year-old woman with a history of antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), autoimmunohemolytic anemia, and recurrent miscarriages presented with rapidly progressive renal insufficiency, dyspnoea, peripheral edema, and blurred vision. Initial workup revealed multi-organ thrombosis, including an ischemic stroke in the right temporal lobe (brain), right central retinal artery thrombosis (eye), deep vein thrombosis in the lower limbs, and left renal vein thrombosis with enlarged kidneys and interstitial edema. Laboratory findings showed anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, elongated APTT, elevated D-dimer, elevated creatinine, and urea. Based on thrombosis in more than three organs within a short period, a diagnosis of Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome (CAPS) was made. Initial aggressive treatment included high molecular weight heparin, high-dose glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone then prednisone), therapeutic plasma exchanges, daily hemodialysis for severe renal insufficiency and anuria, and systemic antibiotics. This led to an improvement in dyspnoea, respiratory failure, hemoglobin, and platelet count, but persistent oliguria required regular hemodialysis. One year after the last Rituximab dose, renal function had significantly improved (creatinine 1.4 mg/dl), and no new thrombotic events were observed. Prednisone was discontinued 2 years after the CAPS presentation.
